title: Tree-structured indexing
lead: ISAM, B+ tree invariants, search, insertion, deletion and variable-length entries.

sections.title: Multilevel indexes and ISAM
sections.html:
A page-sized index node has high fan-out: each separator directs a search to one child page. Repeated index levels reduce the search space by a factor F per level, giving a height proportional to logFN rather than binary search’s log₂N page probes.

ISAM fixes its non-leaf structure when built. Leaf pages initially hold sorted entries; later insertions use the relevant primary leaf or its overflow chain. Deletion can remove entries without changing the non-leaf separators.

This static structure simplifies access to upper levels, but long overflow chains degrade performance as data changes. ISAM is most suitable when updates are limited.

PDF pp. 1–12

sections.title: B+ tree structure and lookup
sections.html:
A B+ tree is balanced: all leaves are at the same depth. Non-leaf keys route searches; leaves contain data entries and are linked for ordered scans. Equality lookup descends to one leaf; range lookup finds its starting leaf and follows leaf links.

In the source’s order-d convention, a non-root node holds d to 2d entries, and an internal node with m keys has m + 1 children. The root has special occupancy rules. High fan-out usually keeps the tree shallow, and upper levels may remain in the buffer pool.

A separator need not be an existing data entry after subsequent deletions; its essential role is to maintain correct child key ranges. Data entries themselves are checked at the leaves.

PDF pp. 13–16

sections.title: Insertion and splitting
sections.html:
Insertion finds the target leaf and inserts in key order. If the leaf overflows, its entries are split between two leaves and a separator is copied up to the parent. The leaf key remains in the leaf because leaves contain the data entries.

If the parent overflows, an internal-node split pushes up the middle separator: it becomes the parent’s routing key and is removed from the split node. Child pointers must be redistributed with the keys. Splitting the root creates a new root and increases the height.

The source insertion of 8* demonstrates both cases: 5 is copied up from the leaf and 17 is pushed up from the internal node. Redistribution to a non-full sibling can sometimes avoid a split, but requires adjusting the parent separator.

PDF pp. 17–20

sections.title: Deletion, occupancy and key compression
sections.html:
After deletion, an underfull node first attempts redistribution with an adjacent sibling sharing its parent. The parent separator must reflect the new boundary. If redistribution is impossible, merge the nodes and remove the corresponding parent entry. Underflow can propagate to the root.

For internal-node merging, the parent separator is pulled down between the two groups of keys and pointers. An empty root can be removed, reducing tree height. Some practical implementations relax minimum occupancy and reclaim only empty pages.

Variable-length entries require byte-based occupancy rather than a fixed entry count. Prefix compression reduces repeated leaf-key prefixes; suffix truncation shortens routing keys while preserving correct comparisons. These optimisations must retain the tree’s search invariants.

PDF pp. 21–30

quiz.question: When the leaf [4,9,12,15,18] splits into [4,9] and [12,15,18], what happens to separator 12?
options: It is removed from every leaf
It is copied into the parent and retained in the right leaf
It is retained only in the left leaf
quiz.explanation: The right leaf starts at 12, so its parent boundary is 12. Copy that boundary into the parent but retain the data entry in the right leaf: a leaf-chain scan must still return 12. Internal-node splitting instead moves a separator up while preserving the leaf data.
